channel.title: Oddly Wired
channel.description: One checked psychology fact a day. Every claim names the study behind it.

item.title: You are more motivated on the first of January.
item.description: A 2014 study found that people seek more 'fresh start' opportunities during temporal landmarks like birthdays or new years.

item.title: You are blind to changes happening right before you.
item.description: In a 1998 study, about half of the participants failed to notice when the person they were talking to was swapped for another.

item.title: The default choice shapes your entire life's direction.
item.description: While researchers like Johnson and Goldstein have shown that default settings correlate with higher registration rates, the actual number of transplants is strongly influenced by healthcare infrastructure, public trust, and logistical coordination, rather than being solely driven by the opt-out default.

item.title: You seek out people who confirm your negative traits.
item.description: A 1983 study showed that people preferred feedback that aligned with their existing self-conception.

item.title: Anxiety about performance can lower your actual results.
item.description: A 1995 study found that black students performed worse on tests when reminded of negative stereotypes about their intelligence.

item.title: Telling you not to do it makes it attractive.
item.description: A 1977 study by Brehm and Weinraub found that restricting access to a toy increased its desirability to children.

item.title: Your brain is outsourcing your memory to technology.
item.description: A 2011 study found that people are less likely to remember facts if they believe they can search them later.

item.title: You assume everyone shares your private opinions.
item.description: A 1977 study showed that people who agreed to wear a sandwich board were more likely to believe others would too.

item.title: You prefer things simply because you see them often.
item.description: A 1968 study showed that participants rated symbols they had viewed more frequently as having a more positive meaning.

item.title: A random number drastically alters your next choice.
item.description: In a 1974 study, spinning a wheel of fortune influenced participants' subsequent estimates of geographical data.

item.title: You believe you are safer than the average person.
item.description: A 1980 study found that most adults rate their personal risk of accidents as significantly lower than their peers.

item.title: You understand your own car less than you think.
item.description: Participants in a 2002 study overestimated their ability to explain how zippers and toilets work.

item.title: You interpret neutral social interactions as deliberate attacks.
item.description: A 1980 study found that highly aggressive individuals are significantly more likely to assume others act with harmful intent during ambiguous social interactions.

item.title: Your ability to make good choices erodes all day.
item.description: A 2011 study observed that judges granted fewer favorable decisions as a decision session progressed, with rates returning to baseline after a break, which researchers suggested may be linked to hunger.

item.title: You ignore information that challenges your existing beliefs.
item.description: A 1979 study found that participants discounted evidence that contradicted their opinions while accepting flawed evidence that supported them.

item.title: Your brain prioritizes threatening information over positive feedback.
item.description: A 2001 review demonstrated that negative events have a stronger and longer-lasting impact on the human psyche than positive ones.

item.title: You value items more simply because they are scarce.
item.description: A 1975 study demonstrated that cookies presented in a scarce supply (two cookies) were rated significantly higher in quality than those in an abundant supply (ten cookies).

item.title: The presence of others makes you less likely to act.
item.description: A 1968 study found that individuals are significantly less likely to intervene in an emergency when they believe others are observing the scene.

item.title: You assign positive character traits based on physical appearance.
item.description: A 1920 study by Edward Thorndike identified a general 'halo effect' in human judgment, where an overall positive impression of a person influences the rating of unrelated specific traits.

item.title: You assume your current project will finish on time.
item.description: A 1994 study of students found they completed senior thesis projects 20 days later than their own most realistic estimates.

item.title: You think your past self knew more than it did.
item.description: A 1975 study by Baruch Fischhoff demonstrated that knowing an outcome significantly impairs the ability to accurately recall one's initial level of uncertainty.

item.title: You believe you see the world exactly as it is.
item.description: The study conducted by Pronin, Lin, and Ross on the bias blind spot was published in 2002.

item.title: You create your own barriers to protect your pride.
item.description: Self-handicapping is the psychological strategy of placing obstacles in your own path to provide an excuse for future failure.

item.title: You value immediate satisfaction more than future success.
item.description: Delay discounting is the tendency to prefer smaller, immediate rewards over larger, delayed rewards. Hyperbolic discounting is a specific mathematical model used to describe how these rewards are discounted over time.

item.title: Your brain misses information for a split second daily.
item.description: The attentional blink is a temporary deficit in reporting a second target when it follows a first target in rapid succession.

item.title: Simply stating your intent makes you act more often.
item.description: The mere measurement effect suggests that asking about intentions can influence subsequent behavior, but the effect is highly contingent on the nature of the task and timing.

item.title: Confidence is often a poor proxy for actual competence.
item.description: The overconfidence effect is the tendency for people to overestimate the accuracy of their own knowledge and the success of their decisions.

item.title: Your opinion of quality depends on what you saw first.
item.description: The contrast effect suggests that your perception of a stimulus is heightened or diminished by the stimulus that preceded it.

item.title: You persist in bad decisions because of past costs.
item.description: The sunk cost fallacy describes the tendency to continue an endeavor once an investment in money, effort, or time has been made.

item.title: You are blind to the obvious when focused elsewhere.
item.description: A 1999 study showed that 46% of the participants failed to see an unexpected object while tracking moving items.

item.title: Your memory will invent details that were never there.
item.description: A 1995 study showed that people frequently report seeing words that were never on a list they just read.

item.title: You judge an idea by how it makes you feel.
item.description: The research on the affect heuristic regarding risk-benefit assessments was established by Finucane, Alhakami, Slovic and Johnson in 2000.

item.title: You remember information better when it relates to you.
item.description: A 1977 study showed that participants recalled adjectives much better when asked if they described themselves.

item.title: You believe your inner emotions are visible to others.
item.description: A 1998 study showed that speakers overestimate how much their nervousness is detectable by their audience.

item.title: You choose a known risk over an unknown one.
item.description: The Ellsberg Paradox shows that people prefer gambles with known odds over gambles where the probability is unknown.

item.title: You do not remember an experience by its total duration.
item.description: A 1996 study showed that retrospective evaluations of pain are determined by the peak intensity and the final moment.

item.title: You will invent reasons for choices you never made.
item.description: A 2005 study showed participants would justify why they chose a face they did not actually pick during a manipulated swap.

item.title: You remember information better if you create it yourself.
item.description: A 1978 study demonstrated that participants remembered words better when they generated them rather than simply reading them.

item.title: Nothing is as important as you think it is.
item.description: A 1998 study showed that students believed living in a sunny climate would significantly boost happiness, despite data proving otherwise.

item.title: Your memory is not a recording, it is a draft.
item.description: A 1974 study found that asking how fast cars were moving when they smashed led to higher speed estimates than asking how fast they were when they hit.

item.title: You judge your actions by circumstances but others by character.
item.description: Research in the 1970s proposed an actor-observer asymmetry in attribution, though modern meta-analyses indicate this effect is often smaller, less consistent, or culturally dependent than early studies suggested.

item.title: You can be nudged into expensive choices by irrelevant options.
item.description: A 1982 study found that adding an inferior decoy option significantly increases the preference for a more expensive premium choice.

item.title: A small blunder makes you more likable, not less.
item.description: In a 1966 study, participants rated an obviously competent person as more attractive when they spilled a cup of coffee.

item.title: You overvalue things just because you own them.
item.description: The endowment effect causes people to place a higher price on items simply because they have gained possession of them.

item.title: You react to the same information differently based on labels.
item.description: The original study used the 'Asian Disease' problem, which asked participants to choose between programs that would save 200 out of 600 lives or result in 400 out of 600 deaths.

item.title: You find it impossible to ignore what you know.
item.description: In Elizabeth Newton's 1990 study, tappers were unable to predict how difficult it would be for listeners to identify a song melody when they could only hear the rhythm being tapped.

item.title: You exert less individual effort when working in groups.
item.description: The phenomenon of reduced individual output in groups is known as the Ringelmann effect, which was later named social loafing in 1979.

item.title: You look more attractive in a group than alone.
item.description: The cheerleader effect causes individuals to be perceived as more physically appealing when viewed as part of a group.

item.title: You prefer a sure gain, even when a gamble pays more.
item.description: The pseudocertainty effect leads people to choose an outcome perceived as certain over a probabilistic one, even when the latter is mathematically superior.

item.title: You complete tasks in the time you allocate, regardless of complexity.
item.description: Parkinson's Law states that work expands to fill the time available for its completion.
